name: Tasmanian, south-eastern language
confidence_why: Crowley and Dixon 1981 call stress placement the most elusive point of Tasmanian phonology and conclude only that any non-final syllable can bear it, Capell 1968 agrees that stress cannot be stated for a language without living speakers, and the lone dissent, Taylor 2006's reading of the nineteenth-century wordlist diacritics as regular initial stress, rests on the same amateur records and is offered by its author as provisional.
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry & R.M.W. Dixon. 1981. Tasmanian. In R.M.W. Dixon & B.J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, vol. 2, 394-421. Canberra: Australian National University Press. (ANU open repository scan, hdl:1885/114846)
catalog_locator: section 2.4 'Stress', p. 413; scope remark section 2.1, p. 407
catalog_quote: The position of stress within a word is perhaps the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology. We have the following source material: [a] Walker marks each vowel with either ¯ or ˘; these marks apparently indicate accent rather than quantity (see the comment in Roth 1899, p.1 of Appendix). [b] Norman uses the same marks, probably in the same way. [c] Milligan says 'when a double consonant or two consonants stand together, the first carries the accent, as in the English words cunningly, peppery, cobbler, pipkin.' This somewhat elusive statement perhaps means that the vowel preceding a sequence of two consonants (in Milligan's orthography) bears stress. [d] Tindale's transcriptions. [e] The Fanny Cochrane Smith recordings. [f] The 1972 Crowley recordings of Mrs. Heffernan and Mrs. Mundy. From these sources it appears that a disyllabic word is always stressed on the first syllable, whereas a trisyllabic word can be stressed on either first or second syllable. Our only general conclusion concerning stress in Tasmanian is thus: any syllable except the last can bear stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: From the 19th-c. stress/emphasis marks (Walker, Norman), Milligan's accent remark, Tindale's transcriptions and the Fanny Cochrane Smith and 1972 Crowley recordings: disyllables carry initial stress; trisyllables carry stress on the first or the second syllable with no recoverable conditioning; stress is never final. No fixed position can be established from the extinct-language records.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said. (Taylor 2006 p.257 explicitly denies an alternating rhythmic cadence for Palawa, but that is his own inference.)
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the disyllable/trisyllable split; Milligan 1859 p.282 (primary) says the syllable before a written double/cluster consonant 'carries the accent', which Crowley & Dixon read as stress on the vowel preceding a CC sequence in his orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress inferred from isolated citation forms in 19th-c. wordlists and from song/speech recordings; the statement is made for 'Tasmanian' as a whole, with the authors noting (p.407) that their phonology is based mainly on the mid-eastern (Oyster Bay/Big River) and south-eastern (Bruny Island) languages. Taylor 2006 (MA thesis, pp. 257-259) instead argues for consistent strong initial stress from the same marks, citing South-East (Bruny, G.A. Robinson) items.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is made for 'Tasmanian' as a whole (Glottolog bookkeeping node tasm1247, retired ISO xtz), not for Bruny Island alone; Crowley & Dixon say (p.407) their phonology rests mainly on the mid-eastern (Oyster Bay/Big River, oyst1235) and south-eastern languages, and their 'South-eastern' language = Bruny Island (brun1235, ISO xpz; sources Robinson, Milligan's 'Brune Island' list, Sterling, Roberts). Of their stress sources, Milligan's accent remark covers his Bruny Island vocabulary directly; Walker's and Norman's marked vocabularies are mostly north-eastern/eastern; the Fanny Cochrane Smith and 1972 recordings are of mixed/uncertain affiliation. The same files and statement serve the sibling tasm1247 record. Language extinct since the 1870s; no instrumental or speaker-based description can exist.

sources.note: p.413: position of stress is 'the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology'; from Walker's/Norman's marks, Milligan's remark, Tindale, the Fanny Cochrane Smith recordings and Crowley's 1972 recordings: a disyllabic word is always stressed on the first syllable, a trisyllable on first or second; only general conclusion: any syllable except the last can bear stress. p.407: the phonology discussion 'is based mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages' (south-eastern = Bruny Island).

sources.citation: Taylor, John Albert. 2006. The Palawa (Tasmanian Aboriginal) languages: a preliminary discussion. MA thesis, University of Tasmania. (section 7.3.3 pp. 138-139; section 7.9 Stress and Accenting pp. 257-259, Table 7.9 with SE = Bruny/G.A. Robinson items)
sources.note: Disagrees with Crowley & Dixon; argues the recorders' macron marked stress and that 'in 99 per cent of word elements in initial position with vowels bearing these diacritics, the first vowel is marked with a bar', i.e. 'strong stressing of the first word element in words' (p. 258); applies Dixon's 'initial syllable is generally stressed' to Palawa but rejects the alternating cadence (p. 257). Amateur philological thesis; pan-Tasmanian, with South-East (Bruny, Robinson) examples.

(primary 19th-c. remark, interpreted by Crowley & Dixon as stress on the vowel before a written CC).
